pr.title: Head each stack segment with its project or a title
pr.head: f14ee414e05b3213e43b6447ff1260c7d9892dea

summary: Projector's site has a Reviews index that lists every pull request with a published summary, and a summary page for each one whose sidebar lists the pull requests in its stack, the chain of dependent pull requests it belongs to. Neither page said what a stack is for. The site did link reviews to projects, but by which plan files a diff touched, so a rename linked to every plan it edited and the upper layers of a stack that implemented a plan linked to nothing.

This pull request carries out the stack-header plan. Each summary now records the one project its pull request carries out, and its name becomes the stack's title. The build takes each stack's members from GitHub's stacks API, splits each stack into segments, one for each run of layers that carry the same project, and draws a header above each segment on both pages. A project header links to the project's page. A stack with no project gets one plain-text title header.

1. A summary records its choice. project is a project name, or "" for none. summary publish refuses a null or missing project, and a name that is empty or longer than 60 characters.
  2. The build finds each stack once. One paginated request lists the repository's GitHub stacks. A pull request in no GitHub stack, and every pull request when GitHub cannot answer, sits on the pull request whose head branch is its base branch, as before.
  3. The build splits each stack into segments. A layer that names no project joins the segment of the layer before it, so a refactor at the bottom of a stack does not hide the project above it.
  4. Both pages draw the headers. The index draws each segment as its own table body under a header row, and the sidebar draws a header above each segment's rows.

cards.title: Terms on this page
cards.html:
• Stack: pull requests that build on one another, bottom first. A pull request alone is a stack of one.
  • GitHub stack: a stack GitHub records, as the gh stack CLI makes it. It keeps its members and their order after they merge.
  • Segment: a run of a stack's layers that carry the same project, drawn under one header.
  • Header: {project, title, url} for a project, or {title} for a stack that carries none.

cards.title: How layers become segments
cards.html:
Projects, bottom firstSegments
A, A, BA: layers 1 and 2. B: layer 3.
A, "", BA: layers 1 and 2. B: layer 3.
"", A, BA: layers 1 and 2. B: layer 3.
A, B, AA: layer 1. B: layer 2. A: layer 3.
"", ""One title segment.

groups.title: A summary records its project and its stack's title
groups.kicker: The new summary field, and the checks publish runs on it
intro: The site cannot tell from a diff which plan a change carries out, so the summarizing agent now records that choice. summary init writes "project": null, which means not decided yet, and summary publish refuses it until the agent sets a project name or "". The summary's name, which every summary already has, becomes the stack's title, capped at 60 characters so it fits a header.
publish does not check that the project exists in the checkout. A pull request that adds a plan records that plan, and the default branch lacks it until the pull request merges.

files.note: Adds repo_stacks, the one paginated stacks request, and require_stack_choices, which publish runs first.

checks.text: repo_stacks raises SummaryError on a 404, on a failed later page, on output that is not JSON, on a page that is not a list, and on empty output, so GitHub answers for every stack or for none. test_a_listing_github_cannot_give_whole_leaves_the_build_none runs each case against a fake gh, and the suite passes at this head.
prepare_page no longer invents a name such as repo#7 summary. An empty name stays empty, so the build can fall back to the pull request's title for a stack's header.

files.note: Covers init, the publish refusals, a project the checkout lacks, a page built alone, and repo_stacks against a fake gh.

groups.title: The build takes stacks from GitHub and splits them into segments
groups.kicker: Who is in each stack, in what order, and under which header
intro: Before this change, the build found stacks only from base branches: a pull request sat on the pull request whose head branch was its base. That loses a layer once its base moves to the default branch, and it breaks a merged stack apart. Now find_stacks asks GitHub first.

1. Inside a GitHub stack, GitHub decides. Each member sits on the member before it in GitHub's order, merged members included, whatever its base branch says.
  2. Everywhere else, base branches decide. A pull request chained by hand onto a GitHub stack's member joins that stack, after its members.
  3. One line reports it. The build prints one stacks: line and never fails or warns over stacks.

stack_segments then splits each stack's members, including members without a summary, into segments. Each pull request's page, entry, and site.json row carry the header of its segment, and each project page lists the reviews in the segments it heads.

checks.text: The index, the sidebar, and the headers all read the one members map that find_stacks returns, so they cannot disagree about who is in a stack.

files.note: Adds find_stacks, github_stacks, stack_segments, and project_header, and narrows project_linker to one project.

checks.text: The walk pushes a member's GitHub successor onto the stack last, so it is visited first, and a GitHub stack's members stay together in GitHub's order before any branch joined by hand. I traced it for #15 based on #9's branch in a stack of #9 and #10, which gives #9, #10, #15, as test_a_pull_request_chained_by_hand_joins_a_github_stack_after_its_members asserts.

A pull request listed in two GitHub stacks stays in the higher-numbered one, and the lower stack closes the gap. Stacks 30 (#9, #10, #11) and 40 (#10, #12) give #9, #11 and #10, #12, which the suite checks.

stack_segments matches the plan's table: a layer with no project joins the segment before it, or the first segment at the bottom, and a project that comes back after another starts a new segment. Traced for alpha, alpha/beta, alpha, which gives three segments.

A summary published before project existed falls back to the first known name in its projects list, then to the one project whose files its diff changes. A diff that touches two projects gets a title header.

files.note: build_checkout hands the build a stacks lookup that returns None whenever repo_stacks fails, as the existing pr_status lookup does.
Build tests for every row of the plan's stack and header tables, and node tests for the index and sidebar markup, including a member without a summary and a merged two-project stack.

checks.text: Each subtest builds a three-layer stack from the recorded projects and checks every page's segments, every page's and row's header, and each project's reviews.

groups.title: The index and the sidebar draw a header above each segment
groups.kicker: Shared header helpers, the index's table bodies, and the CSS
intro: Both pages load summary.js, so the two new helpers live at its top. stackHeaderHtml draws one header: a link for a project, a <span> for a title. stackSegmentsHtml draws the sidebar's stack, a header above each segment's rows, and replaces the old list of project rows.

On the index, reviewsTable groups the rows into stacks as before, then starts a new table body wherever a row's header differs from the row above it. Every body but a stack's last has class="continued" and draws no divider, so the stack still reads as one group.

checks.text: npm ci, npm run check, and npm run build in site/ print no findings and leave the committed JavaScript unchanged. A site built from this repository's summaries draws the #219 and #222 stack as two bodies with one divider in headless Chromium, in both themes, at 1200 and 375 pixels, with no horizontal scroll on the phone.

files.note: Adds stackHeaderHtml and stackSegmentsHtml, and drops projectsList and the page title's name fallback.

checks.text: A stack of one segment keeps the label Pull requests in this stack. With several, each list is labeled with its header's title, so a screen reader names the project each list belongs to.

files.note: reviewsTable draws a table body per segment, and a project page lists its reviews by pull request title.

checks.text: Segments come from comparing the rows drawn. When the Open and Closed boxes hide a whole segment, the segments on either side merge under one header if they name the same project.

files.note: Styles the index's header row and the continued bodies, and keeps the hidden time column at zero width on a phone.

checks.text: The header cell spans all three columns. Without a zero width, the hidden time column would keep its width on a phone and squeeze the titles.

files.note: .prblock .stackhead replaces the old project-row rules, with a three-line clamp and room above every header but the first.

groups.title: The skill, the CLI reference, and the plan
groups.kicker: How an agent makes the two choices, and what the docs now say
intro: summarize-pr now tells the agent to choose project and name at the end of step 4 of "Build the summary", and again in step 2 of the update steps, because a summary published before this change has no project and publish refuses it. Each layer records its own choice and copies no other layer's.

files.note: The two choices: the project the change is about, and two to six words naming the stack's work.
Documents project and the title meaning of name.
Describes stacks from GitHub, the fallback, the stacks: line, segments, and project pages.
Marks the plan completed, settles two details in § 2.2 and § 8.2, and adds § 9, which records that the project shipped and what this repository's build read.

checks.text: Every acceptance row in §§ 4 and 8.5 has a test, and the suite passes at this head. § 9's claims hold: a build from this repository's summaries reads 19 GitHub stacks in 1 request, and with the stacks call answering 404 the build prints the fallback line, finishes, and puts #227 and #231 apart.
